1. Emotion charades: help your child learn about emotions by playing a game of charades. Take turns acting out emotions, and have the other person guess what emotion is being portrayed.

2. Emotion matching: draw different facial expressions on pieces of paper and ask your child to match them with the correct emotion word.

3. Feeling collage: give your child a magazine or brochure and have them cut out pictures of people expressing different emotions. They can then create a collage of different emotions and discuss each one.

4. Emotion reflection: after a frustrating or challenging experience, ask your child to reflect on how they felt and what might help them manage their emotions in the future.

5. Emotional storytelling: read a storybook with your child and discuss the emotions of the characters. Talk about how the characters are feeling and what caused those emotions.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly! Modeling emotional regulation for your child is an essential way to support their emotional development. Here are some tips for modeling emotional regulation:

1. Acknowledge your emotions: Model acknowledging your emotions by labeling them when you feel them. For example, "I feel frustrated right now because I can't figure this out."

2. Take deep breaths: Demonstrate taking deep breaths as a way to calm down when you or your child are feeling upset or overwhelmed.

3. Problem-solve together: Work together with your child to identify solutions to problems that arise in everyday situations. This shows your child how to effectively manage their emotions and find solutions to challenging situations.

4. Role-play: Use pretend play scenarios to practice emotional regulation skills. For example, you could have a "calm down corner" where you and your child practice calming techniques together.

content:Speaker user says: I was out jogging one day when I noticed a person in front of me; about a quarter of a mile ahead. I could tell he was running a little slower than me, and I thought, 'good', I'll try to catch him. I had about a mile to go on my path before I needed to turn off.

After just a few minutes I was only about 100 yards behind him, so I really picked up the pace and pushed myself. One would have thought I was running the last leg of an Olympic event, so determined was I to catch him. And finally I did it! I caught up and passed him by.
On the inside I felt so good. "I beat him!", of course he didn't even know we were racing. And after I passed him, I realised that I had been so focused on competing against him, that I had missed my turn. I had gone nearly six blocks past it. I had to turn around and go all the way back.
Isn't that just what happens in life when we focus on competing with co-workers, neighbours, friends, family - trying to outdo them, or trying to prove that we are more successful or more important? We fail to recognise that we spend our time and energy running after them; and we miss out on our own path to our God given destinies. We compare our journey Home with temporary things, instead of Jesus Christ's example.
ahead of one - someone with a better job, a nicer car, more money in the bank, more education, a more attractive partner, better behaved children, etc. It is therefore very important, and more blessed, to realise that, "You can be the best that you can be, when you are not competing with anyone." - i.e. Just being a better YOU than yesterday.
